intro: Reconstruction has always been shaped by two co-evolving means: the instruments that capture light and position, and the representations into which measurements are turned. New sensors made new representations possible; new representations, in turn, created demand for new kinds of capture. A third layer — computation — mediates between them.

tracks.label: Capture
tracks.description: How images, depth and position are acquired.

tracks.label: Computation
tracks.description: The machinery that turns observations into geometry.

tracks.label: Representation
tracks.description: The form in which the reconstructed world is stored.

items.label: Plate & phototheodolite cameras
items.text: Glass-plate cameras mounted on theodolites gave photographs with known orientation for terrestrial surveying and architecture.

items.label: Stereo photography
items.text: Paired photographs with a known baseline, viewed and measured stereoscopically.

items.label: Aerial film cameras
items.text: Large-format calibrated cameras with fiducials and forward-motion compensation, flown in overlapping strips.

items.label: Metric & réseau cameras
items.text: Cameras with stable, calibrated interior orientation for close-range and industrial measurement; réseau grids corrected film deformation.

items.label: GNSS / INS positioning
items.text: Satellite and inertial navigation observe camera position and attitude directly.

items.label: Digital cameras & sensors
items.text: CCD and CMOS sensors replaced film; digital aerial cameras entered production around 2000–2003.

items.label: Laser scanning (LiDAR)
items.text: Airborne (1990s), terrestrial (2000s) and mobile/handheld (2010s–) scanners measure range directly; a 2020 tablet and phone generation brought small LiDAR sensors to consumers.

items.label: DSLR & mirrorless
items.text: High-resolution interchangeable-lens cameras became the default for close-range photogrammetry and heritage capture.

items.label: Smartphones
items.text: Ubiquitous cameras with inertial sensors, computational photography and, later, depth sensors — the source of internet photo collections and casual captures.

items.label: RGB-D sensors
items.text: Structured-light and time-of-flight depth cameras for real-time dense capture.

items.label: Consumer UAVs
items.text: Low-cost drones with stabilised cameras and, later, RTK positioning made aerial surveys accessible.

items.label: 360° cameras
items.text: Multi-lens spherical cameras for rapid indoor and street capture; require spherical camera models.

items.label: Synchronised multi-camera rigs
items.text: Domes and arrays of genlocked video cameras for capturing dynamic events.

items.label: Video-based multi-view capture
items.text: Continuous video — handheld, egocentric or multi-device — treated as dense spatio-temporal sampling.

items.label: Graphical construction
items.text: Plane-table intersection and perspective constructions by hand.

items.label: Optical–mechanical analogues
items.text: Instruments that physically re-create rays: stereoautographs, stereoplanigraphs, multiplex.

items.label: Electronic computers
items.text: Mainframes and minicomputers for analytical triangulation and analytical plotters.

items.label: Workstations & PCs
items.text: Raster image processing, automatic matching and softcopy photogrammetry.

items.label: Clusters & cloud
items.text: Distributed matching and bundle adjustment for internet-scale collections.

items.label: GPU computing
items.text: General-purpose GPUs accelerated feature extraction, dense fusion and, later, differentiable rendering.

items.label: Deep learning & autodiff
items.text: Automatic differentiation and large-scale training made learned priors and differentiable rendering practical.

items.label: Measured drawings & plans
items.text: Plans, elevations and topographic sheets drawn from intersected points.

items.label: Stereoscopic models
items.text: The perceived, measurable 3D model formed in an oriented stereo instrument — a representation that existed only while being viewed.

items.label: Contour maps & orthophotos
items.text: Height as contour lines; later, differentially rectified orthophotos combining image and map.

items.label: Digital elevation models
items.text: 2.5D height grids and TINs.

items.label: Sparse point clouds
items.text: Triangulated tie points with camera poses — the output of aerial triangulation and SfM.

items.label: Dense point clouds
items.text: Millions of points from dense matching or laser scanning.

items.label: Meshes & textured meshes
items.text: Triangle surfaces with image-derived textures; the standard deliverable for heritage and VFX.

items.label: Voxel grids & TSDFs
items.text: Regular or sparse volumetric grids of signed distance, occupancy or radiance.

items.label: Light fields
items.text: Appearance stored as a sampled function of rays.

items.label: Neural radiance fields
items.text: Continuous learned functions of density and colour.

items.label: Gaussian primitives
items.text: Explicit, differentiable, rasterisable ellipsoids with view-dependent colour.

items.label: Dynamic 4D representations
items.text: Deformation fields, space-time grids and 4D Gaussians.

items.label: Latent & learned scene states
items.text: Implicit scene memories inside networks — emerging and not yet metrological.

couplings.text: Oriented plates made photographs into graphical survey observations.
Stereo pairs plus floating-mark instruments produced measurable 3D models.
Overlapping aerial strips enabled national contour mapping on stereoplotters.
Computers made bundle adjustment of large blocks — and sparse point sets with poses — feasible.
Digital imagery allowed matching to generate DEMs automatically.
Direct ranging produced dense point clouds independent of image texture.
Internet photo collections forced SfM to handle uncalibrated, unordered imagery.
Cheap aerial imagery drove SfM–MVS textured meshes and orthomosaics in surveying.
Real-time depth streams were fused into GPU voxel TSDFs.
GPU autodiff and fused kernels made radiance-field optimisation practical.
Tile-based GPU rasterisation is what makes Gaussian splatting real-time.
Synchronised multi-view video supplies the observations dynamic representations need.
Casual video plus learned priors pushes 4D reconstruction toward monocular capture.
Large-scale training produces scene states that are inferred rather than measured.
Reverse influence: automated SfM made consumer and DSLR cameras acceptable for measurement, changing what equipment surveyors buy.
Reverse influence: Gaussian splatting created consumer capture apps and new capture protocols.
